text: Earlier in the course we built the smallest possible agent: the model proposes a tool call, the harness runs it, and the result is appended to the context, over and over until the model answers. Real agents use the same loop. What separates a demo from a dependable agent is how the loop behaves when things go wrong, when arguments are malformed, when a tool returns an enormous output, or when the model keeps going round in circles.

Start with the tools themselves. Each tool is described by a name, a sentence of explanation, and a schema for its arguments, and that description is effectively part of the prompt, because the model reads it to decide when the tool is useful and how to call it. Writing the description well matters as much as writing the function. Generating the schema directly from the function's signature keeps the code and its description from drifting apart.

Before running a call, the harness checks its arguments against the schema. When something is wrong, or the tool itself raises an error, the loop does not crash. Instead the error is written back as an observation in plain words, such as a missing argument called date, so the model can read it and try again. It is the difference between a warning light on the dashboard and an engine that seizes.

Observations also need a size limit. A single tool can return an entire log file, megabytes of text that would crowd everything else out of the context window. The harness therefore truncates long results, keeping the beginning and the end with a note about what was removed, or it stores the full output elsewhere and returns a short handle, which the agent can use to page through the rest only if it needs to.

An agent normally stops when the model replies without asking for a tool, but that alone is not enough. Every loop also needs budgets: a maximum number of steps, of tokens and of time, after which it halts and reports what it managed to do. It is also worth detecting repetition, because an agent that issues the same call with the same arguments twice in a row is usually stuck rather than making progress.

It is worth asking whether a task needs an agent at all. If the steps are known in advance, a workflow, where ordinary code calls the model at fixed points, is cheaper, faster and easier to test. An agent earns its place when the path cannot be predicted, so the model has to decide the next step from what it has just observed. And whichever you build, actions that cannot be undone, such as payments or deletions, should wait for a person's confirmation.

Long tasks bring a new problem. Every step adds an observation to the transcript, and after enough steps the transcript no longer fits in the context window, while well before that it has become slow and expensive to reread. The next lesson looks at how long running agents manage their context and their memory.
